title: Is the Third Word a Shuffle of the Other Two?

concept.title: A table over how many letters were taken from each of the two words
body: The word `c` is an **interleaving** of the words `a` and `b` if it can be obtained by taking all the letters of `a` and all the letters of `b` and **merging** them, so that the letters of each word keep their order. For `a = aabcc`, `b = dbbca` and `c = aadbbcbcac` the answer is yes; for `c = aadbbbaccc` it is no.

Build `c` from left to right. After `i + j` letters of `c`, we have used the first `i` letters of `a` and the first `j` letters of `b` (the number of letters used from `b` follows from `i`). Let `ok(i, j)` be true if the first `i + j` letters of `c` can be made from the first `i` letters of `a` and the first `j` letters of `b`. The last letter of that prefix of `c` came either from `a` (it must equal `a[i]` and `ok(i - 1, j)` must hold) or from `b`: **`ok(i, j) = (ok(i - 1, j) and a[i] = c[i + j]) or (ok(i, j - 1) and b[j] = c[i + j])`**, with `ok(0, 0)` true. If the lengths do not fit (`|a| + |b| != |c|`), the answer is no at once.

The 2D table collapses to **one row**: `ok[j]` before the update is `ok(i - 1, j)` (from `a`), `ok[j - 1]` after the update is `ok(i, j - 1)` (from `b`). This is a path counting problem in disguise: a way to interleave is a monotone path from the corner `(0, 0)` to `(|a|, |b|)` in the grid, where each step uses the next letter of `a` (down) or of `b` (right). The time is O(|a| * |b|), at most a million steps.

statement: Three words `a`, `b` and `c` are given. Print `yes` if `c` can be obtained by merging all the letters of `a` and all the letters of `b` (each word keeps the order of its letters), otherwise print `no`.
inputFormat: The first line has the word `a`.
The second line has the word `b`.
The third line has the word `c`.
constraints: 1 <= length of a, length of b <= 1000
All words consist of lowercase English letters.

examples.note: Take a a (from a), d b b (from b), c (a), b c (b), a... a valid merge exists: yes.
No merge gives this word: no.

hints: Let ok(i, j) say whether the first i + j letters of c can be made from the first i letters of a and the first j letters of b.
The last letter came from a or from b; check that it matches and that the shorter prefix is ok.
If the lengths do not add up, the answer is no.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

a = input().strip()
b = input().strip()
c = input().strip()

# Your code here

explanation: ok(i, j) tells whether the first i + j letters of c can be built from the first i letters of a and the first j letters of b: the last letter came from a (it must match and ok(i - 1, j) must hold) or from b (it must match and ok(i, j - 1) must hold). One row is kept; the answer is ok(|a|, |b|).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

a = input().strip()
b = input().strip()
c = input().strip()

n = len(a)
m = len(b)
if n + m != len(c):
    print("no")
else:
    ok = [False] * (m + 1)
    ok[0] = True
    for j in range(1, m + 1):
        ok[j] = ok[j - 1] and b[j - 1] == c[j - 1]
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        ok[0] = ok[0] and a[i - 1] == c[i - 1]
        ai = a[i - 1]
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            ch = c[i + j - 1]
            ok[j] = (ok[j] and ai == ch) or (ok[j - 1] and b[j - 1] == ch)
    print("yes" if ok[m] else "no")
